candidate_workflows: Choose an observable user outcome that indicates satisfaction, then rank or prioritize opportunities by economic value multiplied by demonstrated outcomes instead of bids or stated intent alone.

When a buyer or incumbent ignores a technically superior feature, test whether its current revenue model makes the improvement economically unattractive before treating the reaction as a product verdict.

In the essay's 2006 context, separate the policy question of what patent law should be from the operating question of how a startup acts under the rules then in force; retain the author's explicit uncertainty rather than converting experience-based advice into categorical doctrine.
Before enforcing intellectual property against a competitor, weigh the likely legal gain against lasting reputation damage among technical people and other stakeholders.

As a historical early-software-startup heuristic, keep product quality and user growth ahead of speculative infringement anxiety and tie patent filings to an explicit defensive, scaling, or acquisition rationale.

As a dated acquisition heuristic, combine a growing user base with protectable critical technology in a build-versus-buy case while recognizing that integrated design and execution may be the stronger moat.
title: Are Software Patents Evil?

candidate_workflows: When interpreting a surprising action or outcome, compare an intent-centered explanation with a simpler situational or random explanation and prefer the account that does not center the observer unless evidence supports it.
Treat apparent purpose or malice as a hypothesis rather than signal; state what observation would distinguish deliberate action from noise before updating a startup decision.
title: See Randomness

candidate_workflows: Release a stable, minimal version quickly, use the launch to expose product and team flaws, and ship small improvements from user reactions every day or two.
Explain and show the product's value immediately to a casual visitor, then track whether those visitors convert and whether growth improves.
Maintain a startup risk register that prioritizes internal disputes, inertia, and ignored users over visible incumbent threats or routine operating disasters.
Hold the goal firmly while changing tactics and even direction in response to evidence; distinguish determination from attachment to the initial plan.

When a category seems exhausted, test whether present products could plausibly remain unchanged for decades and whether meaningful wants remain unsatisfied; do not infer a ceiling from current competitors or acquirer capacity.
Assume proposed funding, acquisition, and customer deals may fail, keep alternatives and product progress alive until close, and build leverage by not depending on any single deal.
Evaluate the stress of founding not only against possible wealth but against its potential to compress the time spent making a living and create more future autonomy.
title: The Hardest Lessons for Startups to Learn

candidate_workflows: Audit a prospective startup hub for its limiting human reagent: capable technical founders or experienced investors who add selection judgment, advice, and connections as well as capital.
Do not use offices or technology parks as proxies for an ecosystem; focus on whether small founder teams can form, fund, and remain in the place.
Attract a critical mass through excellent peers, a strong university, a livable town, and tolerance for unusual ideas rather than top-down startup theater.

Seed a small expert cluster and measure the multi-year flywheel in which startup employees become founders and successful founders become investors; allow time for the chain reaction to become self-sustaining.
title: How to Be Silicon Valley

candidate_workflows: Evaluate a startup ecosystem across immigration access, university quality, employment flexibility, incorporation burden, initial-market reach, and early angel capital rather than reducing it to entrepreneurial attitude.
Replay the histories of successful startups under a jurisdiction's actual rules and remove any requirement that would have killed them during their fragile apartment-or-garage stage.
Treat flexible career changes and visible founder examples as activation infrastructure: expose capable people to peers who have started companies and preserve permission to change course.
Benchmark a startup hub like a competing product for mobile founders and investors, then improve the concrete experience of living, moving, working, and building there.
title: Why Startups Condense in America

candidate_workflows: Before deferring to a field's insiders, inspect whether its selection tests measure real output or reward test-hacking, politics, and appearances; look for a later customer or product test that is harder to game.
Use outsider status to bracket a problem with risky ideas while the downside and visibility are low, and judge experiments by what works rather than whether they initially look respectable.
Keep direct contact with the medium and span a vertical slice across design, implementation, and users so discoveries do not get lost at organizational handoffs.
Explore neglected new platforms with small, inexpensive projects, cycle quickly, and publish directly to an audience that can supply real resistance and feedback.
title: The Power of the Marginal

candidate_workflows: Run the island test on a founder or maker's work setup: imagine being unable to obtain anything for a weekend, list the nonessential items that still must be packed, and treat them as dependencies to protect or examine.
Separate momentum work that can survive ambient noise from generative work that requires quiet, and keep a low-friction capture tool available so remembering one idea does not block the next.
title: The Island Test

candidate_workflows: Choose product, writing, or company references from things the team genuinely uses, enjoys, or learns from rather than things it merely believes it should admire.
Remove status and presentation cues from a reference, ask whether it would still be chosen in an ordinary setting, and use private or guilty preferences as additional evidence of authentic taste.
When borrowing a model, identify the causal qualities that make it effective and avoid copying visible flaws, fashionable mannerisms, or artifacts of age.
title: Copy What You Like

candidate_workflows: Open with one concrete sentence explaining what the company built and why users want it; prefer a narrow intelligible description that can be expanded over a vague description of all future possibilities.
When a demo fits the format, show the user's problem and how the product resolves it rather than touring features, and prepare for predictable technical failure.
Assign the strongest speaker to address the audience while another person operates the product; keep resumes, competition, and tentative business-model detail subordinate to the product and problem.
Rehearse slow conversational delivery, cut every nonessential slide word, and stay candid about what is not yet known instead of imitating a mature corporation.
Select a few company-specific numbers, concrete user stories, and a memorable descriptive phrase that together provide evidence of demand and focus.
title: How to Present to Investors

candidate_workflows: Decide when to start by examining commitment, escape hatches, obligations, and the direction of peer pressure rather than age alone; deliberately choose peers and milestones that push toward real output.
Preserve room to recover from wrong ideas by living and operating cheaply, designing affordable products, and allowing the plan to evolve before scaling spend.
Choose cofounders from people already known under real work, favor recurring builders who finish projects, and keep promising collaborations alive while gaining experience.
Before carrying side-project work into a startup, review employment agreements and code provenance, obtain written releases when appropriate, and avoid using code that may belong to a prior employer.

Learn startups by working inside one and by shipping useful software to real users; treat early implementation as an instrument for refining the problem rather than as a class project graded by effort.
title: A Student's Guide to Startups

candidate_workflows: Run failure reviews backward from the question of whether the company is making something users want, then identify which team, product, launch, capital, or commitment behavior is blocking that outcome.
Form a compatible multi-founder team with strong technical judgment; investigate early misgivings and define vesting and departure paths before conflict makes them expensive.

Include location in the startup pre-mortem by comparing access to experts, hiring pools, supporting services, ambitious peers, and norms sympathetic to founders; relocate when the gap is materially constraining.
Generate ideas from specific unsolved problems, and evaluate pivots by user excitement and whether each step reuses learning or assets instead of repeatedly restarting.

Treat platform selection as a structural risk: have strong technical founders benchmark real constraints and scaling behavior, and inspect what leading builders use before committing to a conventionally respectable choice.
Launch the smallest core that is useful by itself and expandable, then use specific target users and measured responses as instruments when founder intuition does not apply.
Translate funding into runway to the next visible milestone, keep burn and hiring low, and hire first for building product or reaching users.

Model how capital changes pace, direction, and control; manage investors without surrendering the product, and require full founder effort only after honestly assessing whether the opportunity deserves it.

Assign at least one technical founder explicit responsibility for finding users, selling, partnerships, or other business work until the company can support specialization; a product and idea alone do not create demand.
title: The 18 Mistakes That Kill Startups

candidate_workflows: Define a product or creative work's intended audience and purpose, then compare alternatives by how reliably they produce the intended response rather than declaring quality wholly subjective.
Separate authentic audience reaction from brand, finish, social pressure, and manipulative presentation by removing context, repeating exposure, and explicitly cataloging recurring tricks.
Broaden the reference set across user segments, cultures, and time periods to reduce local bias while retaining a demanding standard for whether the work performs its purpose.
title: How Art Can Be Good

candidate_workflows: During the earliest stage, preserve direct maker work, fast individual decisions, and close collaboration; measure progress by product output and learning rather than corporate-looking activity.

Audit rituals of professionalism such as formal dress, staged office hours, presentation volume, and report production, and remove any that consume energy or conceal how the team actually produces its best work.
Use first-hand founder accounts to calibrate expectations about the strange, informal shape of productive early startup work instead of imitating mature-company operations.
title: Learning from Founders

candidate_workflows: Classify work as choosing among bounded alternatives or inventing within an open-ended search space; lean more on experience and self-discipline for the former and curiosity plus hard-problem practice for the latter.

Do not treat the absence of a clear upper bound in creative work as evidence of failure; interpret recurring discontent as a possible cost of pushing the frontier and compartmentalize it from everyday sadness.
Develop distinctive capability by selecting a genuine idiosyncratic curiosity, sustaining work on hard problems, and giving makers an appreciative but difficult-to-impress audience.
title: Is It Worth Being Wise?

candidate_workflows: Decompose reluctance to start into separate objections, then test each for evidence instead of treating a mixed feeling of uncertainty as one verdict.
Assess readiness through adult responses to hard work and challenge, demonstrated ownership of self-directed projects, commitment capacity, independence, and concrete family or financial constraints.

Treat a missing cofounder as a formation problem: work with capable people before partnering, preserve school and project relationships, relocate if necessary, and reconsider an idea no one good wants to join.
Generate an initial idea from a narrow but genuine need in the founders' own lives, and weight demonstrated building ability above the first idea because the idea will change.

For each real constraint, design a lower-risk path such as joining a startup or starting with a revenue-producing service, while recognizing when the commitment and structure of a startup are genuinely unwanted.
Identify job-taking as a default rather than an axiom and compare it consciously with the risks, learning, autonomy, and time horizon of founding.
title: Why to Not Not Start a Startup

candidate_workflows: When inherited fear of an incumbent shapes company positioning, re-evaluate its present power from current founder behavior and market evidence rather than reputation formed in an earlier platform era.
Triangulate a power shift from user-facing product breakthroughs, architecture and distribution changes, enabling infrastructure, and the tool choices of technically demanding early adopters.

When considering an incumbent response to a platform shift, compare acquiring strong autonomous startup teams with building internally, and account explicitly for the legacy culture's ability to neutralize acquired talent.
title: Microsoft is Dead

candidate_workflows: Before interpreting a hiring, investment, accelerator, or partnership decision, ask whether the evaluator is trying to estimate the company accurately or merely select an adequate option from a crowded pool.
Treat rejection from a selection process as noisy evidence rather than a precise verdict; investigate any underlying product or team signal without personalizing the outcome.
Design a pitch or application to surface decisive evidence quickly instead of assuming a busy selector will discover hidden merit unaided.
title: Two Kinds of Judgement

candidate_workflows: Choose angels or VCs by stage, check size, risk tolerance, advice quality, and desired exit scale rather than treating all outside capital as interchangeable.
Model an investor from the incentives of their fund, partners, portfolio, reputation, and peer firms; use that model to predict what evidence and outcomes they will optimize.
Select the amount and valuation by runway needs, dilution, control, and realistic exit optionality, not by the status signal of the largest check or headline valuation.
Treat a termsheet as the start of the closing phase, keep competing relationships and product momentum alive, and continue selling the deal until funds arrive.
Compare founder concentration risk with an investor's diversified portfolio incentives before accepting advice to reject an acquisition, take a kill-or-cure bet, or prolong the company.
Budget fundraising as a major interruption, interpret an ambiguous investor response as no unless a termsheet exists, and maintain a cheap executable backup plan so no single investor is required.
title: The Hacker's Guide to Investors
